source.title: Assessing Muscular Strength in Youth: Usefulness of Standing Long Jump as a General Index of Muscular Fitness

paper.citation: Castro-Piñero, J., Ortega, F. B., Artero, E. G., Girela-Rejón, M. J., Mora, J., Sjöström, M., & Ruiz, J. R. (2010). Assessing muscular strength in youth: Usefulness of standing long jump as a general index of muscular fitness. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 24(7), 1810–1817. https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181ddb03d
paper.abstract: How strongly is standing long-jump performance associated with other lower- and upper-body strength tests in youth? Ninety-four healthy Caucasian children and adolescents, including 45 girls, aged 6–17 years. School/population fitness context rather than trained collegiate athletes. Applicability to collegiate American football is indirect because maturation, training history, and sport specialization differ. Cross-sectional association study comparing standing long jump with vertical, squat, and countermovement jumps plus basketball throw, push-ups, and isometric strength. Multiple-regression models adjusted for sex, age, and BMI in the combined sample. Best trials were retained, so the study assesses between-test association rather than responsiveness to training or readiness.
paper.tldr: This paper informs low-cost field testing of muscular fitness in children and adolescents. Standing long jump was strongly associated with other lower-body explosive-strength tests, with reported R² values of 0.829–0.864. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional association study comparing standing long jump with vertical, squat, and countermovement jumps plus basketball throw, push-ups, and isometric strength. Multiple-regression models adjusted for sex, age, and BMI in the combined sample. Best trials were retained, so the study assesses between-test association rather than responsiveness to training or readiness.
paper.findings: Standing long jump was strongly associated with other lower-body explosive-strength tests, with reported R² values of 0.829–0.864. In the combined sample, standing long jump explained 85.1% of basketball-throw variance, 54.2% of push-up variance, and 69.4% of isometric-strength variance after adjustment. The authors concluded that standing long jump could serve as a practical general muscular-fitness index in youth, but this reflects association rather than criterion validity for every strength quality.
paper.limitations: The sample was relatively small and pubertal status was not measured. Jump distance depends on anthropometry, coordination, and technique as well as force-generating capacity. Strong shared variance does not make the standing long jump interchangeable with upper-body or maximal-strength tests. Cross-sectional results do not establish sensitivity to training change, injury status, or individual decision thresholds.
paper.practicalImplications: Standing long jump is a useful low-cost screening measure when broad youth muscular fitness is the decision target. In trained collegiate athletes, use it as one task-specific output and retain direct measures when maximal strength, upper-body capacity, or change over time is the actual decision.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, standing long jump is a useful low-cost screening measure when broad youth muscular fitness is the decision target. In trained collegiate athletes, use it as one task-specific output and retain direct measures when maximal strength, upper-body capacity, or change over time is the actual decision. Preserve the study population and avoid converting one finding into a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
